checkpoints: A batching data loader only collapses keys that get registered within the same event-loop tick (the batch dispatch window) into one call; once that window closes, any further `load()` calls open a new window of their own.

Awaiting a `load()` call inside a `for...of` loop fully pauses that iteration until the promise resolves, so the next iteration's `load()` call happens on a later tick — this closes the batch window after exactly one key every time, even though the loader's batch function and scope are configured correctly.

N single-key batch lines in the data-source log (`[BATCH] ... IN ('<one-id>')` repeated N times) instead of one combined multi-key line is the fingerprint of broken batching — it is N+1 in disguise, N sequential round-trips happening despite a batching loader being wired up.

The root cause lives in the calling code's control flow, not in the loader's configuration: the loader itself, its batch function, and its request scope are not the source of the bug, so 'fixing' the loader's setup would not resolve the slowdown.

The fix is to register every `load()` call before awaiting any of them, so all keys land in the same tick: mapping over the collection to start every `load()` synchronously and only then awaiting them together (e.g. with a single combined wait over all the pending calls) lets the loader batch them into one `IN (...)` query.

Turning the related field into its own field resolver that returns the loader's pending call directly, without an `await` inside that resolver, is the more idiomatic fix — the GraphQL engine itself invokes that field once per parent within the same execution tick, so all the resulting `load()` calls naturally land in the same batch window without any manual `Promise.all`.

The loader's per-request cache deduplicates a key that gets loaded twice within the same request, but that is a separate mechanism from batching by width; since every key in this scenario is unique, the cache cannot mask or fix a sequential-await bug like this one.

Proving the fix requires counting batch-log lines for the same nested query before and after (N single-key lines collapsing to one multi-key line) and re-measuring latency against the size of the parent list (linear growth flattening out), then locking in a regression test that asserts exactly one batch-log line per relation per request so the sequential-await bug cannot silently return.
